_comment: The ONE authority of published-contract maturity.
This is contractual policy, not roadmap state and not an operational status. It answers
exactly one question per published module: may its public ABI change, and under what
conditions. It is deliberately NOT DSL_SURFACE_MANIFEST: that manifest classifies
constructors in the pipeline authoring surface, and this classifies the artifacts an
external CONSUMER compiles against. Reusing it would conflate a DSL function with a
library ABI and quietly make the stricter policy apply to the wrong surface.
Taxonomy (the canonical one; nothing outside it is accepted):
STABLE                 breaking is forbidden except across an explicit major boundary
PARTIAL                additive changes allowed; breaking needs a recorded exception
EXPERIMENTAL           breaking allowed under a recorded decision with a stated boundary
DEPRECATED             members may be removed only after the declared removal boundary
UNSUPPORTED_FAIL_CLOSED the construct refuses itself; there is no compatibility surface
Read by a human reviewer: no task in the build enforces this file, so a module published
without an entry here is not caught automatically. A deliberate breaking change is recorded,
not discussed, in the SIBLING file published-contract-exceptions.json: one entry per break,
carrying the module, the commit sha, the surface, the change, the permitting maturity, the
reasoning and the removal boundary. This pointer used to read "See publishedContractExceptions()
in the same test", which named a function that does not exist and sent the reader to the
wrong file for a ledger that was one directory away.
SURFACES. A module is not one thing. `contracts` above is the module-level DEFAULT,
and it exists because a flat EXPERIMENTAL on every module is not a decision: it is a blanket
that lets the next change ride on it without saying what it is riding on. `surfaces` below is
where the guarantee genuinely DIFFERS from the module default, and a surface entry must beat
the module on evidence or not exist.
Resolution is: effective(module, surface) = surfaces[module][surface] if declared, else the
module's own classification. Nothing is inherited implicitly and nothing is inferred from the
package name.
The four rules that make this classification mean something. NOT one of them is enforced by a task

today: the fitness test that used to check them was removed with the rest of the testing reset, and nothing replaced it. They are the reviewer's checklist, not a gate, and this file says so rather than claiming an enforcement that does not exist:
1. `covers` must resolve in BOTH independent authorities — the module's published .api dump
and DSL_SURFACE_MANIFEST.md. One authority alone is forgeable: the ABI proves the symbol
ships, the manifest proves what it means. A family that names something invented in
either file fails the build.
2. A surface may be STRICTER than its module. It may not be MORE PERMISSIVE. Refinement that
loosens the policy is not refinement, it is an escape hatch with a longer name.
3. An exception may not invoke a maturity looser than the effective one at its surface.
4. UNSUPPORTED_FAIL_CLOSED hosts no exceptions, because a construct that refuses itself has
nothing a consumer could have depended on. That is the whole meaning of the classification.

pipeline-domain: EXPERIMENTAL, and the reason is specific rather than convenient: this module is the
innermost seam and its types are re-exported through pipeline-events and
pipeline-scripting-api, so almost every change to it is additive-by-necessity rather
than by choice. The one class of change this repository made repeatedly in P3-E is
enriching an internal decision ADT with evidence the producer already had
(WaitUntilReconciliationDecision.Aborted gained the attempt it had been discarding into
a string). That is a real breaking change to a published data class, and pretending
otherwise would make the classification a description of what we wish were true.
Promoting it to STABLE requires that the decision ADTs stop being part of the external
surface — i.e. that consumers resolve outcomes through event projections rather than
reaching for domain ADTs directly. That is S5.4's work, and until it lands the honest
pipeline-scripting-api: EXPERIMENTAL: the DSL is the authored authoring surface and several of its constructs
are already deprecated with a declared replacement (catchError, LFC1-007), which is the
signature of a surface still converging.
pipeline-events: EXPERIMENTAL: the wire vocabulary is published and load-bearing, and this block is
actively changing it (typed projections, fail-closed decoders). It is not a frozen
contract yet, and calling it one would only defer the work.
pipeline-output: EXPERIMENTAL: the smallest of the four and the least consumed; nothing in the P3-E
pipeline-runtime-api: EXPERIMENTAL, and the reason is specific rather than convenient: this module is new in
0.52.0-rc1 (carved out of :pipeline-runtime by the M.0 module-split commit 2a97653a)
and carries the three M2 publish/subscribe ports (RuntimeRecoverPort, RuntimeControlPort,
RuntimeIntrospectionPort) plus the pure decider (RuntimeRecoverDecision) and their
sealed ADTs. The module's public ABI is fully implemented in the M.0 commit and backed by
the in-monorepo adapter test suites (RuntimeRecoverPortAdapterTest, RuntimeControlPortAdapterTest,
but it has not been certified by pipelinek-release-harness and no external consumer has
compiled against it yet. EXPERIMENTAL is the honest classification: the surface is stable
in shape (interfaces, sealed ADTs, refusal cases) and unstable in the sense that the next
certified release may add FABRIC capability checks per port. The capability flips from
EXPERIMENTAL to PUBLISHED at the candidate boundary the publication plan §2.1 documents,
and a deliberate breaking change would be recorded in the sibling
pipeline-credentials-api: EXPERIMENTAL, and the reason is specific rather than convenient: this module is NOT
published as a Maven coordinate - it resolves from no repository, and it is absent from
the published SDK - but its bytes DO travel with every release, inside the product's
own distribution ZIP, as lib/pipeline-credentials-api-<version>.jar. A module whose
bytes are published is a published surface even when it is not a resolvable
coordinate, so the rule that decides a break of it is the same rule that decides a
break of a contract: EXPERIMENTAL, breaking allowed under a recorded decision with a
The second reading of the ABI compares this module against the JAR that the previous
distribution shipped, so a break of it is a fact the door can name instead of a fact
only the tree's own committed baseline can see. The receipt for such a break is an
entry of published-contract-exceptions.json, and it carries the census that shows
who was reachable: the module has no consumer outside this repository, because no
external consumer resolves it and the examples resolve only the published SDK.
What this classification does NOT do is promote the module: it does not add it to the
SDK, and it does not make its ABI a promise to a consumer that does not exist. It says
that the bytes travel, and therefore that changing them is a versioned break that has
to be recorded rather than a quiet edit.
pipeline-service-client: EXPERIMENTAL, and the reason is specific: this module is the FIRST artifact that
speaks the local service's wire from the OUTSIDE. Until it existed, the vocabulary of
the wire lived inside the product and no consumer could resolve it, so a client had to
copy the codec and a copy was free to drift from it. The module is published, so its
bytes are a promise to whoever resolves it, and it carries the wire's own types:
a change of a request's shape, of a refusal's name or of the run.state document is a
breaking change of a PUBLISHED contract.
Its first publication is also the first release whose previous surface is EMPTY: the
previous release's SDK repository does not carry this artifact, so there is no previous
surface to compare against and everything this artifact publishes is an addition. The
second reading of the ABI says so in its verdict rather than refusing to compare,
and the refusal it used to make is kept for the case that is a refusal: a previous
release whose repository could not be read.
EXPERIMENTAL is the honest classification because the wire's version is still /2 and no
external consumer has compiled against this artifact yet. It flips to PUBLISHED at the
candidate boundary the publication plan documents.
THE SURFACE THIS ARTIFACT PUBLISHES IS THE WIRE, AND NOW THE WIRE CARRIES AN
AUTHORIZATION. Every request presents a credential in the `auth` field, and the refusals
it can be answered with have NAMES: `not-authorized`, `run-not-authorized` and
`too-many-subscriptions`. The first publication of this artifact therefore freezes a line
that carries an authorization, and that is the decision the entry in the sibling ledger
records. The `auth` field is OPTIONAL in the grammar - a line without it is answered
`not-authorized` and not `incompatible-protocol` - because the schema of the protocol is
still /2 and the version identifies the SHAPE of the line, not the policy the service
applies to it.
WHAT THIS ARTIFACT DOES NOT PUBLISH, on purpose: the vocabulary of WHAT a client may ask
about (`all`, `none`, a list of run ids). It lives in the application, and it is not
published because it has to grow with the slices that bring new rights - starting a run,
cancelling a run, answering a question a run is waiting for - and every one of those would
add a case to a SEALED interface that a published artifact already carries. Publishing the
scope now would freeze a vocabulary whose next case is already known, and a frozen scope
would make those slices versioned breaks of an ABI that consumers already resolve.
THE SURFACE THIS ARTIFACT PUBLISHES NOW ALSO CARRIES A START. The wire can ask for a run
and not only ask about one: the operation `run.start` and the six negatives with name
that answer it (`start-not-authorized`, `script-not-admitted`,
`workspace-not-admitted`, `idempotency-conflict`, `too-many-supervised-runs` and
`run-start-refused`). A supervisor that could only ask would have to launch the run
itself, over a path the service does not own, and the authority over the process would
leave the service that owns the runs. The answer is an IDENTITY and not a result
(`runId`, `correlationId`, `ownerId`, `startedAtMs`): the child prints them after it takes
its lease, so a client that is told 'started' is told about a run that exists.
The right to START is still NOT in this surface, and this slice is the reason it was worth
keeping it out: the vocabulary of WHAT a client may do lives in the application and grew
there (`all+start`, `none+start`), while the published artifact grew only with the
operation and with the names of the refusals it can be answered with. The next right will
arrive the same way, and publishing the scope would freeze a vocabulary whose next case is
already known.
THE SURFACE THIS ARTIFACT PUBLISHES NOW ALSO CARRIES A CANCEL. The wire can close a run
and not only ask about one or start one: the operation `run.cancel` and the two negatives
with name that answer it (`cancel-not-authorized` and `run-cancel-refused`). A client that
started a run over the socket had no way to stop it - the run outlives the connection that
asked for it - and a socket that started runs without being able to close them would be a
half-published authority. The answer is the TERMINAL of the run and it is durable when the
answer travels, so the client reads a fact and not an EOF; a repeated cancellation answers
the same terminal with `already-cancelled`, because a run is closed once and not twice.
The right to CANCEL is still NOT in this surface, and this slice is the second reason it was
worth keeping it out: the vocabulary of WHAT a client may do lives in the application and
grew there (`all+start+cancel`), while the published artifact grew only with the operation
and with the names of the refusals it can be answered with. The right grew as a SET inside
the application - `WithRights(over, granted)` - precisely so that adding a right did not
add a case to a published sealed interface: the next right will arrive the same way, and
publishing the scope would freeze a vocabulary whose next case is already known.
THE SURFACE THIS ARTIFACT PUBLISHES NOW ALSO CARRIES A CONFIGURATION. The wire can ask
for a run WITH the environment its steps will see: the operation `run.start` gained the
optional field `configuration`, a map of names to plain texts, and the answer returns the
same map back. The ECHO is the reason and not a courtesy: the schema of the protocol does
not change when an operation gains a field, so a service that does not know the field
ignores it in silence and starts the run without the configuration, and a client that sent
it believes in a configuration that is not there. The echo turns that silence into a fact,
and the typed client that compares the echo with what it sent turns the fact into a named
negative - a refusal of the wire's own shape, not an exception.
THE CONFIGURATION IS A PUBLIC CHANNEL AND THE ARTIFACT SAYS SO, in the refusal as much as
in the documentation: there is no oracle that tells a secret from a plain text, so the wire
cannot promise to keep one. What it refuses, BY NAME, is the vocabulary of the product: the
three prefixes the service and the launcher own, the names the sandbox removes from an
environment, and the three names the launcher consumes to build the PATH of a step. Those
are refused with the single new word `run-configuration-refused` and the reason inside it,
because a vocabulary that grew with the rules would multiply the published words without
giving the client more power. The right to start still governs it, and no new right was
published for it: the configuration travels inside a start request, so it is part of
starting.

guarantee: These four are ACCEPTED SYNTAX THAT ALWAYS FAILS CLOSED, and they are the only
published surfaces in this repository where that is true.
The manifest pins each one: `git` and `load` are ATOMIC_STEP with no handler and no
descriptor row, so admission rejects before any effect; `node` and `ansiColor` lower to
core.node / core.ansiColor with no descriptor row, so compile/validate rejects; the
`retry` retrofit points at the block form and throws IllegalArgumentException.
Why they are not merely EXPERIMENTAL, which is what the module says as a whole: there is
no consumer program that can contain a working call to any of them. Compatibility is a
relation between a shipped artifact and a caller that got a value out of it. A construct
whose every call path ends in a refusal has no such caller, so there is nothing to freeze
and nothing to break. Calling that EXPERIMENTAL would be exactly the blanket this layer
exists to replace — it would promise a stability guarantee for a guarantee that does not
The practical consequence is the direction that matters: removing or reshaping these four
does NOT need a recorded exception, while touching any other surface of
promotion_precondition: Promotion here means IMPLEMENTING, not re-describing. The classification stops being
UNSUPPORTED_FAIL_CLOSED on the day the construct acquires a handler, a descriptor row and
an interpreter that can succeed — the same three things `agent` needed before it left
this state in S3.1. Promoting it without them would be classifying a stub as a contract.
